visual.lectureScript:
This is the last teaching unit, and it uses most of what you have learned. Hedging from Units 7 and 17, connectors from Unit 6, evidence from Unit 14, sources from Units 16 and 17, and register from Unit 18.
First pattern: the three parts of an argument.
An argument has a claim, evidence, and a warrant.
The claim is what you want somebody to accept. We should replace the system.
The evidence is what supports it. It failed eleven times last year.
And the warrant is the assumption that connects them — the reason the evidence counts as support for the claim.
Here, the warrant is something like: a system that fails eleven times a year is unreliable enough to justify the cost of replacing it.
Almost nobody states the warrant. Most arguments consist of a claim and evidence, with the connection left implicit, and that is usually fine because the warrant is obvious and shared.
But here is why it matters. When two people disagree and neither can understand the other, it is almost always the warrant they disagree about, not the evidence.
You say it failed eleven times, so replace it. They agree it failed eleven times. They do not agree that eleven failures justifies forty thousand pounds. The evidence is not in dispute at all, and both of you keep repeating it.
So the practical move is: when an argument is stuck, state your warrant out loud. I am assuming that eleven failures a year is enough to justify the cost. Is that where we disagree?
That sentence resolves more arguments than any amount of additional evidence, because it locates the actual disagreement.
And when you are building an argument, ask what you are assuming. If your warrant is something your reader might not share, it needs to be stated and supported like anything else.
Second pattern: persuasive devices, and where they stop being honest.
English has a set of standard devices and they are all legitimate in their honest use.
Repetition, for emphasis. The same phrase returned to at intervals.
The rule of three. Shorter, cheaper and more reliable. Three items have a rhythm that two and four do not, and every language has noticed this.
The rhetorical question. Why has nobody asked the warehouse team? — a question you are not expecting answered.
Anecdote, which makes an abstract point concrete. One story about one delivery will be remembered when the statistics are not.
And understatement, which in English is unusually powerful. The results were not encouraging can be stronger than the results were terrible, because it invites the reader to supply the strength themselves.
Now the line, and it is a real one.
Anecdote becomes dishonest when it is used as evidence rather than as illustration. One story shows that something can happen. It does not show how often, and presenting it as though it does is the commonest way a persuasive piece misleads.
The rhetorical question becomes dishonest when it assumes something unproved. Why has nobody asked the warehouse team is fine if nobody has. Why is management ignoring safety assumes a conclusion and dresses it as a question, and the reader who nods has agreed to something they were never shown.
Repetition becomes dishonest when it substitutes for evidence. Saying something four times does not make it more supported, and it does make it more believed, which is precisely the problem.
And cherry-picking — selecting the evidence that supports you and omitting the rest — is the one that does not have an honest version. Everything else on this list can be used well.
Third pattern: rebutting a counter-argument.
This is the move that separates a considered position from a stubborn one, and it has a shape.
State the strongest version of the other side. Not a weak version — the strongest. If you can only defeat a weak version, you have not defeated anything.
Concede what is true in it. Almost every serious counter-argument contains something true.
Then show why it does not settle the question. Usually because it is outweighed, or because it applies only in some cases, or because it rests on a warrant you can challenge.
The strongest argument against replacing the system is cost — forty thousand is real money and the budget does not have it. That is true, and it would be decisive if the failures were stable. They are not: they have risen each year for three years, so the comparison is not forty thousand against nothing, it is forty thousand against a rising cost we have not counted.
Notice what that does. It gives the other side its best case, agrees with the true part, and then locates precisely where it fails.
And notice what it is not. Arguing against a weak version of the other side — a strawman — is the most common failure, and it is usually accidental rather than dishonest. You argue against what you imagine somebody thinks rather than what they actually said, and anybody who holds the real position can see immediately that you have not addressed it.
The test is simple and uncomfortable: could somebody who holds the opposing view read your version of it and say yes, that is what I think?
If not, you are not arguing with them.
Go to Patterns.

readings.title: The Part Nobody States
readings.passageScript:
An argument has three parts and almost every argument states two of them.
The claim is what you want accepted. We should replace the system.
The evidence is what supports it. It failed eleven times last year.
The warrant is the assumption connecting them — the reason the evidence counts as support for the claim. Here it is something like: eleven failures a year is unreliable enough to justify forty thousand pounds.
Nobody states the warrant, and usually that is fine. When it is obvious and shared, saying it aloud would be pedantic.
But here is why it matters, and it is the most practically useful idea in this unit.
When two people disagree and neither can understand the other, it is almost always the warrant they disagree about — not the evidence.
You say it failed eleven times, so replace it.
They agree it failed eleven times. They do not agree that eleven failures justifies forty thousand pounds.
So the evidence is not in dispute at all, and both of you keep producing more of it. You find the failure log. They already believe the failure log. Nothing moves.
The move that unsticks this is to state your warrant out loud.
I am assuming that eleven failures a year is enough to justify the cost. Is that where we actually disagree?
That sentence resolves more arguments than any additional evidence, because it locates the disagreement instead of restating the case.
And when you are building an argument rather than having one, the question to ask yourself is: what am I assuming that my reader might not?
If the warrant is shared, leave it implicit. If it is not, it needs stating and supporting like anything else — because an unstated warrant that your reader does not accept means your evidence does no work at all, however good it is.

readings.passageScript:
English has a standard set of persuasive devices and every one of them has an honest use.

Anecdote crosses it when used as evidence rather than as illustration. One story shows that something can happen. It does not show how often. readings.title: The Same Case, Twice
readings.setting: Two versions of the same recommendation, written by the same person a week apart.
readings.passageScript:
VERSION A

  We have to replace the system. It failed
  eleven times last year - eleven times.
  How much longer are we expected to work
  around a system that nobody trusts?

  Last month it went down during the
  Thursday run and Dani lost four hours
  rebuilding the manifest by hand. Four
  hours. Anybody who has stood in that
  warehouse knows this cannot continue.

  Some people will say it is too
  expensive. But we cannot put a price on
  reliability, and the people arguing
  against this are the people who never
  have to use it.

-----------------------------------------

  VERSION B

  I am recommending we budget to replace
  the system next year.

  It failed eleven times in the last
  twelve months, against three in the
  preceding year and one the year before
  that. The trend matters more than the
  number.

  I am assuming that a failure rate rising
  this steeply justifies the cost. If we
  disagree, that is where.

  The strongest argument against is cost:
  40,000 is real and it is not in this
  year's budget. That would be decisive if
  the failure rate were stable. On the
  current trend we would expect around
  twenty failures next year, at roughly
  four hours each - about 80 lost hours,
  which is most of the difference.

  One caveat: the four-hour figure comes
  from one incident that I timed. The
  others were not recorded.

grammar.title: Claim, evidence, warrant
grammar.explanation: An argument has three parts and almost everybody states two. The missing one is where disagreements actually live.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
THE THREE PARTS
  CLAIM    what you want accepted
     We should replace the system.
  EVIDENCE what supports it
     It failed eleven times last year.
  WARRANT  the assumption connecting them
     Eleven failures a year is unreliable
     enough to justify the cost.

NOBODY STATES THE WARRANT.
  Usually fine - it is often obvious
  and shared.

BUT WHEN AN ARGUMENT IS STUCK
  it is almost always the WARRANT that
  is disputed, not the evidence.

  You: it failed eleven times, so replace it.
  Them: agreed it failed eleven times.
        Not agreed that eleven justifies
        40,000.
  ^ more evidence changes NOTHING.

THE MOVE THAT UNSTICKS IT
  \"I am assuming that eleven failures a
   year justifies the cost. Is that where
   we disagree?\"

WHEN BUILDING AN ARGUMENT
  ask: what am I assuming that my reader
  might not? If they might not share it,
  state and support it.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to argue for replacing a system.
1. Claim: we should replace it.
2. Evidence: it failed eleven times last year.
3. Now find the warrant. Ask what has to be true for the evidence to support the claim.
4. Something like: a failure rate of eleven a year makes a system unreliable enough to justify forty thousand pounds.
5. Is that shared? Not necessarily — somebody who thinks eleven failures is tolerable, or that forty thousand is unaffordable, accepts your evidence and rejects your claim.
6. So state it: I am assuming that a failure rate this high justifies the cost. If we disagree, that is where.
Now the same move in a stuck argument. You have produced the failure log three times and nothing is moving.
1. Ask whether they dispute the log. They do not.
2. So the disagreement is not evidential.
3. State your warrant and ask. The argument either resolves or becomes specific, and either is better than repeating.
grammar.commonMistake: Responding to disagreement with more evidence. If the warrant is what is disputed, additional evidence is answering a question nobody asked, and the argument repeats indefinitely. The other error is leaving a warrant implicit when the reader does not share it — the evidence then does no work at all, however strong it is.
grammar.memoryTip: Find the assumption connecting evidence to claim. State it when you are stuck.
grammar.practice:
For each, name the claim, the evidence and the unstated warrant.
1. We should replace the system. It failed eleven times last year.
2. She should get the job. She has ten years' experience.
3. We should close the site. It made a loss for three years.
4. The policy has failed. Numbers have not fallen.
5. He is not suitable. He arrived late twice.
6. We should buy the cheaper one. It costs half as much.
grammar.answerKey:
1. Warrant: eleven failures a year is unreliable enough to justify the replacement cost.
2. Warrant: ten years' experience is the relevant qualification for this job — which is disputable if the job needs something experience does not supply.
3. Warrant: three loss-making years means the site will not become profitable, and profitability is the criterion.
4. Warrant: this policy was the main thing acting on those numbers, and enough time has passed for an effect to show.
5. Warrant: lateness twice predicts unsuitability — a warrant most people would reject as too weak for the claim.
6. Warrant: the two are equivalent in everything except price, which is exactly what Unit 15 said is often false.
Numbers 4 and 5 have the weakest warrants, and in both the evidence is not in doubt. That is the pattern: the argument is contestable at the warrant while the evidence is agreed.
Number 6 is the price-and-cost distinction from Unit 15 reappearing as an unstated assumption.

grammar.title: Persuasive devices and their limits
grammar.explanation: A standard set of devices, all legitimate in their honest use, each with a line — and one with no honest version at all.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
THE DEVICES, HONESTLY USED

  REPETITION      for emphasis
  RULE OF THREE   shorter, cheaper,
                  more reliable
  RHETORICAL Q    Why has nobody asked
                  the warehouse team?
  ANECDOTE        makes a point concrete
  UNDERSTATEMENT  "not encouraging" - the
                  reader supplies the
                  strength
  APPEAL          to fairness, to
                  consequences

THE LINES
  ANECDOTE -> dishonest as EVIDENCE.
     One story shows something CAN happen,
     not how OFTEN.
  RHETORICAL Q -> dishonest when it
     ASSUMES something unproved.
  REPETITION -> dishonest when it
     SUBSTITUTES for evidence. Four times
     is not better supported; it is more
     believed.
  APPEAL -> a fallacy when it REPLACES
     the reasoning.

ONE HAS NO HONEST VERSION
  CHERRY-PICKING. The reader cannot
  detect it from the text.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to make a point about a system failure vivid.
1. Choose an anecdote: last month it went down during the Thursday run and a colleague spent four hours rebuilding the manifest by hand.
2. That is legitimate — it makes an abstract failure rate concrete and it will be remembered.
3. Now check the line. Are you presenting it as illustration or as evidence?
4. If your case rests on the eleven failures and the story shows what one of them was like, that is illustration and it is honest.
5. If your case rests on the story and eleven is mentioned once, you have used an anecdote as evidence — and one incident tells the reader nothing about frequency.
6. The test: remove the anecdote. If the argument collapses, it was doing evidential work it cannot support.
Now a rhetorical question. Why has nobody asked the warehouse team?
1. Has anybody asked them? If not, the question is legitimate and pointed.
2. Compare: why is management ignoring safety? That assumes management is ignoring safety, which has not been shown.
3. The difference is whether the embedded assumption is established. The form is identical.
grammar.commonMistake: Using an anecdote as evidence, which is the commonest way a persuasive piece misleads and is usually not deliberate — the writer is genuinely moved by the story and does not notice it is carrying the argument. The other error is treating all appeals to feeling as fallacies; an appeal to fairness or to consequences is a proper part of an argument about what should be done, and only becomes a fallacy when it replaces the reasoning.
grammar.memoryTip: Anecdote illustrates, it does not establish. Cherry-picking has no honest version.
grammar.practice:
For each, say HONEST or NOT, and why.
1. One story about a four-hour failure, used to illustrate a rate of eleven.
2. One story about a four-hour failure, as the main support for replacing the system.
3. Why has nobody asked the warehouse team? (nobody has)
4. Why is management ignoring safety? (not established)
5. Repeating eleven times twice, for emphasis.
6. Reporting three years from a twenty-year series, chosen because they support you.
grammar.answerKey:
1. HONEST — illustration. It makes the rate concrete and the argument survives without it.
2. NOT — one incident says nothing about frequency, and here it is carrying the case.
3. HONEST — the embedded assumption is true and the question is pointed.
4. NOT — it assumes the conclusion and disguises it as a question. A reader who nods has agreed to something unshown.
5. HONEST — emphasis is a legitimate use of repetition, provided the figure is supported elsewhere.
6. NOT — cherry-picking, and it is the one device with no honest version.
Numbers 1 and 2 are the same anecdote doing two different jobs. The test is whether the argument survives its removal.
Numbers 3 and 4 are the same grammatical form, and the difference is entirely whether the embedded assumption has been established.

grammar.title: Rebutting a counter-argument
grammar.explanation: The move that separates a considered position from a stubborn one. It has a shape, and one uncomfortable test.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
THE SHAPE

  1 STATE the strongest version of the
    other side. Not a weak version.
  2 CONCEDE what is true in it. Almost
    every serious objection contains
    something true.
  3 SHOW why it does not settle the
    question - outweighed, limited in
    scope, or resting on a warrant you
    can challenge.

WORKED THROUGH
  "The strongest argument against is cost.
   40,000 is real and unbudgeted. That
   would be decisive if the failure rate
   were stable. It is not - it has risen
   for three years."

THE STRAWMAN
  arguing against a WEAK version.
  Usually accidental: you argue with what
  you IMAGINE they think.

THE TEST - short and uncomfortable
  could somebody who holds the opposing
  view read your version and say
  "yes, that is what I think"?

  If not, you are not arguing with them.
grammar.workedExample:
You are arguing to replace a system and somebody will object on cost.
1. State their strongest version, not the weakest. The weak version is people will say it is expensive. The strong version is: forty thousand is real money, it is not in this year's budget, and committing it means something else does not happen.
2. Concede what is true. All of that is true, and if the failure rate were stable it would be decisive.
3. Now show why it does not settle it. The failure rate is not stable — it has risen for three years — so the comparison is not forty thousand against nothing. It is forty thousand against a rising cost that has not been counted.
4. Apply the test. Could somebody who objects on cost read step one and say yes, that is my position? If they would, you have engaged. If they would say I never said that, you have built a strawman.
Compare what Version A in Reading 3 does: some people will say it is too expensive, but we cannot put a price on reliability. That states the objection in its weakest form, concedes nothing, and answers it with a slogan.
grammar.commonMistake: Stating the other side's position in its weakest form, which is usually accidental rather than dishonest — you argue against what you imagine somebody thinks rather than what they said. It convinces nobody who holds the real view. The other error is refusing to concede anything, which makes the whole argument read as advocacy rather than analysis and invites the reader to look for what you have left out.
grammar.memoryTip: Strongest version, concede what is true, then show why it does not settle it.
grammar.practice:
For each objection, write the three steps: strongest version, what is true in it, why it does not settle the question.
1. Replacing the system is too expensive.
2. The new rota is unfair to weekend staff.
3. We should not consult the team; it will raise expectations.
4. One failure is not a pattern.
grammar.answerKey:
Model answers.
1. Strongest: 40,000 is real, it is not budgeted, and committing it displaces something else. True: all of it, and it would be decisive if failures were stable. Why not settled: failures have risen for three years, so the comparison is against a rising uncounted cost rather than against nothing.
2. Strongest: weekend staff lose two guaranteed weekends a month under the new cycle, and they were not asked. True: both, and the second is a process failure regardless of the outcome. Why not settled: the alternative cycles all remove something from somebody, and this one distributes the loss most evenly — but the consultation point stands and should be fixed separately.
3. Strongest: consulting people about a decision that is effectively made does raise expectations and then disappoints them, which damages trust more than not asking. True: that is a real risk and it has happened here before. Why not settled: the decision is not made, and the team hold information about the weekend pattern that the decision needs.
4. Strongest: one incident could be a coincidence, and acting on a single case wastes effort and credibility. True: entirely — one anecdote is not a rate. Why not settled: this is not one failure but eleven, of which one was timed; the anecdote illustrates rather than establishes.
In every one, step two concedes something genuinely true. If a step two is empty, the objection was probably stated in its weak form.
Number 4 is worth noticing: the objection is correct as stated and the rebuttal works by correcting a misreading of the case rather than by defeating the principle.

writing.title: Writing 1 — An argument in full
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Choose a position you actually hold about something at work, in your study, or in public life.
Write the argument in about 350 words.
State the claim in the first two sentences.
Give evidence, cited so a reader could check it.
State your warrant explicitly.
Rebut the strongest counter-argument using the three steps.
Include at least one caveat that weakens your own case.
Use at most two persuasive devices and name them at the end.
Then write two lines: what your warrant is, and whether you think your reader shares it.
writing.modelText:
I am recommending we budget to replace the loading system next year rather than in three years as currently planned.

It failed eleven times in the last twelve months, against three in the preceding year and one the year before. Those figures come from the maintenance log, which is on the shared drive. The trend matters more than the number.

I am assuming that a failure rate rising this steeply justifies the replacement cost of about 40,000. If we disagree, that is where the disagreement is, not in the figures.

The strongest argument against is cost. Forty thousand is real money, it is not in this year's budget, and committing it means something else does not happen. That is all true, and it would be decisive if the failure rate were stable. It is not. On the current trend we would expect around twenty failures next year, at roughly four hours each — about eighty lost hours, which is most of the difference between the two options.

One caveat, and it matters. The four-hour figure comes from a single incident I happened to time. The other failures were not recorded, so the eighty-hour projection rests on one measurement repeated. It could be substantially wrong in either direction.

I would also concede that replacing a system creates its own disruption, which I have not costed at all.

What I am confident about is the direction: eleven, three, one is a trend, and nothing has changed that would explain it stopping.

Devices used: the rule of three in eleven, three, one — which is a real sequence and not a rhetorical arrangement. And understatement in it could be substantially wrong, where I could have said the projection is unreliable.

1. My warrant is that a steeply rising failure rate justifies pre-emptive replacement rather than waiting for the planned date.
2. I think the finance side does not share it. They would accept every figure and argue that a rising rate justifies monitoring rather than spending, which is a genuine position and the one I would need to answer next.
writing.successCriteria: Claim in the first two sentences; evidence cited so it could be checked; warrant stated explicitly; a rebuttal using all three steps with a genuine concession; at least one caveat weakening the writer's own case; at most two devices, named; two lines identifying the warrant and judging whether the reader shares it
writing.support: Write the counter-argument first, in its strongest form, before you write anything of your own. Doing it in that order makes it much harder to produce a strawman, because you have not yet committed to a position you need to defend.
writing.extension: Give it to somebody who disagrees and ask whether your version of their objection is one they recognise. That is the only real test of step one.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Diagnose an argument
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Find a real persuasive piece — an opinion column, a campaign page, a business case, a letter to a newspaper.
Write a diagnosis of about 250 words.
Identify the claim, the evidence and the warrant.
Name every persuasive device used.
Say which devices are used honestly and which are not, with a reason for each.
Identify anything cherry-picked or misrepresented.
Then say whether the conclusion might still be true despite the flaws.
writing.modelText:
The claim is that the council should reverse the parking charges introduced in March.

The evidence is that four businesses on one street have closed since then, and that a survey of 60 traders found 80 per cent opposed to the charges.

The warrant — never stated — is that the closures were caused by the charges and that trader opinion should decide the policy. Both are contestable, and the second is a genuine argument the piece never makes.

Devices. An anecdote about one baker who closed after nineteen years, which is used as evidence rather than illustration: it carries the whole emotional weight and shows only that one business closed. A rhetorical question — how many more must go before the council listens? — which assumes the causal link the piece has not established. Repetition of nineteen years three times. And an appeal to consequences for named local people, which is legitimate and properly done.

Cherry-picking. The piece gives closures since March and no figure for closures in any earlier period, so the reader cannot tell whether four is high. It also does not say how many businesses are on the street.

Misrepresentation. It says the council claims the charges have no effect, and no such claim is quoted.

Could the conclusion still be true? Yes. The charges may well have harmed those businesses, and the piece has not shown it. A weak argument for a claim is not evidence against the claim, and the diagnosis says nothing either way about whether the policy should be reversed.
writing.successCriteria: Claim, evidence and warrant all identified, with the warrant stated in words the original does not use; every device named; an honest-or-not judgement with a reason for each; at least one instance of cherry-picking or misrepresentation identified; a final judgement separating the quality of the argument from the truth of the conclusion
writing.support: Find the warrant by asking what would have to be true for the evidence to support the claim. In persuasive writing it is almost never stated, and it is usually the most contestable thing in the piece.
writing.extension: Write the strongest version of the opposing case in three sentences. If the piece had done that, would it have been more persuasive or less?

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read the two versions
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Use the two versions in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. What is Version A's repetition doing, and is it adding support?
2. What is wrong with the final sentence of Version A?
3. Quote Version B's warrant and say what stating it achieves.
4. Why does Version B include a caveat that weakens its own case?

writing.modelText:
1. It is creating emphasis. Eleven times and four hours are each said twice, and the repetition makes them more memorable without making them better evidenced. Nothing in it is untrue, and it is the device crossing the line described in Reading 2 — more believed rather than more supported.
2. It says the people arguing against this are the people who never have to use it. That attacks the position of the objectors rather than the objection, and it is also a strawman, since nobody in the piece is quoted as arguing anything. It makes disagreement look like bad faith and closes the discussion rather than advancing it.
3. I am assuming that a failure rate rising this steeply justifies the cost. If we disagree, that is where. It locates the possible disagreement in advance, so a reader who disagrees knows exactly what to respond to instead of restating the figures — which is precisely the deadlock Reading 1 describes.
4. Because the four-hour figure rests on one incident that the writer timed and the rest were not recorded. Stating it means the reader learns the limitation from the writer rather than discovering it later, and it makes the other figures more credible by showing that the writer distinguishes between what is measured and what is estimated.
5. Version B, to a reader who has to decide. Version A is more forceful and gives a decision-maker nothing to act on except a mood: it has one comparison, no trend, no costed alternative, and it treats the main objection as bad faith. Version B supplies a trend, a stated assumption, a costed rebuttal and its own limitations, all of which are what somebody signing off forty thousand pounds actually needs. Force and persuasiveness are different things when the reader has to justify a decision afterwards.

writing.support: Count what a decision-maker could act on in each version. Version A has one incident and a figure. Version B has a trend, a projection, a costed comparison and a stated uncertainty. That count is most of the answer to question 5.
writing.extension: Version B's caveat could have been left out and nobody would have known. Write two sentences on why including it was still the right choice.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the twelve
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Every item has exactly one fault from this unit.
Rewrite it and say which pattern it came from.
1. It failed eleven times, so we should replace it. (the reader may not share your assumption)
2. I have shown you the failure log three times now. (they do not dispute the log)
3. Last month it went down and Dani lost four hours. This proves the system is unreliable.
4. Why is management ignoring safety? (this has not been established)
5. It is unacceptable. It is completely unacceptable. It is simply not acceptable. (as the argument)
6. Sales rose in 2019, 2021 and 2023. (2020 and 2022 fell and are not mentioned)
7. Some people will say it is too expensive, but we cannot put a price on reliability.
8. The people arguing against this never have to use it.
9. Nobody could seriously argue that we should just do nothing. (nobody argued that)
10. The argument is a fallacy, so the conclusion is false.
11. It is necessary because it is required.
12. I accept none of the points against this. (one of them is true)
writing.modelText:
1. It failed eleven times, and I am assuming that rate justifies the replacement cost. (Pattern 1 — state the warrant)
2. You do not dispute the log. I think we disagree about whether eleven failures justifies the cost — is that right? (Pattern 1 — more evidence answers a question nobody asked)
3. Last month it went down and Dani lost four hours, which is what one of the eleven failures looks like in practice. (Pattern 2 — anecdote illustrates, it does not prove)
4. Has safety been raised with management, and what was the response? (Pattern 2 — a rhetorical question must not assume the conclusion)
5. It failed eleven times against three the year before. (Pattern 2 — repetition cannot substitute for evidence)
6. Sales rose in three of the last five years and fell in two. (Pattern 2 — cherry-picking)
7. The strongest argument against is cost: 40,000 is real and unbudgeted. That would be decisive if failures were stable. (Pattern 3 — state the strong version and concede)
8. Delete it. (Pattern 3 — it attacks the objector rather than the objection)
9. The strongest version of the do-nothing case is that the current rate is tolerable and the money is better spent elsewhere. (Pattern 3 — strawman)
10. The argument is a fallacy, so it does not establish the conclusion — which may still be true. (Pattern 2 — naming a fallacy is not refuting a claim)
11. It is necessary because the failure rate has tripled in two years. (Pattern 1 — circular; supply a real reason)
12. I accept the cost point and dispute the conclusion. (Pattern 3 — concede what is true)

writing.support: Numbers 7, 8, 9 and 12 are all card 3 failing in four ways: a weak version stated, an attack on the person, an invented position, and a refusal to concede. Fix them together and the shape becomes clear.
writing.extension: Number 10 is the one that most people get wrong in both directions. Write one example of a bad argument for a true conclusion, and one of a good argument for a false one.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Find the warrant
activities.instructionsAndItems:
For each, write the unstated warrant, then say whether you would expect a reader to share it.
1. We should replace the system. It failed eleven times last year.
2. She should get the job. She has ten years' experience.
3. We should close the site. It made a loss for three years.
4. The policy has failed. Numbers have not fallen.
5. He is not suitable. He arrived late twice.
6. We should buy the cheaper one. It costs half as much.
7. The training worked. Nobody has complained.
8. We should consult the team. They will be affected.
9. The supplier is unreliable. One delivery was late.
10. We should keep the old system. Everybody knows it.
11. The report is wrong. It was written quickly.
12. She is the strongest candidate. She interviewed best.
activities.answerSummary:
1. Eleven failures a year justifies the replacement cost. — contestable; a finance reader may not.
2. Ten years' experience is the relevant qualification here. — contestable if the role needs something experience does not supply.
3. Three loss-making years predicts continued losses, and profitability is the criterion. — the second half is often disputed.
4. This policy was the main thing acting on those numbers, and enough time has passed. — usually contestable, and Unit 17's third possibility applies.
5. Lateness twice predicts unsuitability. — most readers would reject this as far too weak.
6. The two are equivalent in everything except price. — Unit 15 says this is usually false.
7. Absence of complaint indicates success. — weak; people frequently do not complain.
8. Being affected entitles you to be consulted. — many would share this, and it is a value rather than a fact.
9. One late delivery indicates a pattern. — one case is not a rate, as Unit 17 says.
10. Familiarity outweighs the system's faults. — contestable and rarely stated.
11. Speed of writing predicts inaccuracy. — weak, and it attacks the process rather than the content.
12. Interview performance predicts job performance. — widely assumed and genuinely disputed.
The weakest warrants are in 5, 7, 9 and 11, and in every one the evidence is not in doubt. That is the pattern this exercise exists to show.
Number 8's warrant is a value rather than a factual claim, and those are the warrants most worth stating — people disagree about values openly and productively, and about hidden ones not at all.
